title: How Royal Bank of Scotland Identifies Fraud in the Contact Center - Results by the Numbers
description: Jason Costain,  Head of Fraud Strategy and Relationship Management at Royal Bank of Scotland discusses their recent deployment of Nuance Security Suite to help combat fraud attacks. 3634-2

asr.full_text: Brings intelligence to life. Bring intelligence to life. I'm Jason Costein and head of Fraud Strategy for Royal Bank of Scotland and that involves managing our fraud defence systems to optimise them to ensure that we defend against fraud threats What we were trying to do was identify fraud within our telephony channel but we knew that the channel was being used to perpetrate fraud elsewhere in all the channels. But also had the aim of trying to reduce and disrupt the effect of organised criminals, because we were aware that we're being attacked by the same individuals time and time again. This isn't about fraud loss in the telephony channel, people think the payment from telephony is where we can save money. We only lose a couple of million pounds in that channel. How big can the benefit be? Think more broadly and what you start to see are huge benefits. In the first year we have screened over 17 million calls. You know I think now the latest stats are showing me that with 1 in 3500 calls that we receive is fraudulent into our contact centre. We identified a very prolific fraudster, making thousands of calls a month. We are able to use the Fraud Miners solution to identify that fraud voice and the calls and accounts have been associated with. From taking those accounts, we were able to then use other technology we have to look at the devices that we've seen on those accounts that we believe the fraudster was using, and that will that led us to five different devices associated with that voice and then those devices we then data mined and we identified over 1,500 other bank accounts where we'd seen suspect logins from those devices. So there is a significant additional intelligence payoff from startling with fraud miner. And that just shows the value that comes in addition with fraud savings and those accounts really were accounts that were either potential victims or they were money mules, so from one prolific fraudster identified through Nuance, you get to protect one in half thousand victims. In using that technology and that intelligence, what it started to do, was give us the payback we were looking for, which was the social benefit of disrupting organised criminals and we've already seen a couple of arrests from that particular criminal network. It's only the foot soldiers and mules, as they start to be interviewed what that will do is give us a better picture of who these organised criminals are. So when we added all that up we're expected to save a reasonable amount of money and we've probably saved one and a half times that. And in terms of ROI for the tool, so the amount of money we spent deploying it versus the benefit we've received in fraud savings the ROI is probably well over 300 percent so as a deployment of technology and a payback it's been very impressive.

textual.observation: The speaker describes identifying a prolific fraudster through contact-center calls, associating the fraud voice with calls and accounts, linking those accounts to five devices, and finding suspect logins on more than 1,500 other bank accounts.

textual.context: This is presented as a bank's retrospective fraud-detection account, with the speaker describing defensive identification and disruption rather than promoting the activity.
textual.potential_relevance: The stated relationship between repeated contact-center calls, associated devices, suspect logins and bank accounts may be relevant for later review of a described fraud mechanism.
textual.limitations: The records do not establish the identities of the callers, the specific login activity, the ultimate disposition of the accounts, or that any particular account holder experienced a loss.

textual_context_notes.observation: The source frames the subject as fraud prevention and defense against attacks.

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it presents a case-study discussion of Royal Bank of Scotland using Nuance security technology to identify fraud in contact-center calls. The fraudster, suspect logins, account-device links, ROI, and fraud-savings figures are described as part of the bank's defensive investigation and reported performance metrics, not as an offer to viewers. The closing branding and website reference identify a corporate context rather than soliciting payments, private data, or participation in fraudulent conduct.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The speaker discusses operational use of a fraud-detection tool to identify a suspected fraud voice, associate calls and accounts with it, and identify suspect logins from related devices. The reported ROI is framed as a technology-deployment result, not as an investment offer to viewers.
